title: Render each asset tag once per manifest
body:
`stylesheet_link_tag`, `javascript_include_tag`, `image_tag`, `favicon_tag` and `javascript_importmap_tag` rebuilt their HTML on every render, about 6.9 KB per page in a generated layout, although a production manifest never changes.

Each `Amber::Assets::Manifest` now owns a `RenderedTags` store. A tag for a logical path without extra attributes, and an import map, is rendered once and then returned as the same `String`. A manifest reloaded in development comes with an empty store, so a rebuilt asset gets a fresh tag. A missing asset raises as before and stores nothing. Tags with attributes and public URLs (`/...`, `https:`, `data:`) are rendered as before and not stored, and each kind stores at most 1,024 tags, so call sites that pass varying paths cannot grow it without bound. The stored import map key is a copy, so a caller that edits its hash afterward gets a fresh render.

## Measurements
Harness: `home-page-memory-bench` (`mem.rb`) on an app from Amber CLI main with the Post scaffold and 50 seeded rows; `crystal-alpha build --release` (Crystal 1.21.0, LLVM 21.1.8), arm64 macOS, production mode, one process. Route `/b/lean/full`: the 2,577-byte home page, fully rendered (view, layout and its three asset tags) through Error and SecurityHeaders only. Before = amber v2-dev 814705ee, after = this branch. Three rounds per starting heap, interleaved ABBA; medians; oha, 32 connections, 20 s. The machine was shared with heavy jobs (load average 40 to 270), so requests/s is approximate.

| Starting heap | Metric | Before | After |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| any | Bytes allocated per request (sequential, 10,000 requests) | 22,752 | 16,112 (-6,640) |
| 16 MiB (today's generated default) | Server CPU per request | 24.6 µs | 17.7 µs |
| | Requests/s | 20,082 | 25,046 |
| | p50 | 0.80 ms | 0.57 ms |
| | Peak RSS | 22.03 MiB | 22.06 MiB |
| 8 MiB (amber_cli#60's default) | Server CPU per request | 26.6 µs | 17.8 µs |
| | Requests/s | 15,683 | 24,495 |
| | p50 | 0.83 ms | 0.58 ms |
| | **Peak RSS** | **13.33 MiB** | **16.34 MiB** |
| 0 | Requests/s | 22,817 | 23,614 |
| | p50 | 0.77 ms | 0.62 ms |
| | **Peak RSS** | **13.56 MiB** | **16.50 MiB** |

## Why this is not merged
Peak RSS rises by 3.0 MiB on this route at an 8 MiB or 0 starting heap, in every one of the 6 runs. Live data after a collection is the same (4.1 MiB on both sides). The collector grows its heap once, by a third (8.0 to 10.7 MiB), within the first second of load, and the before build never does: with fewer small allocations per request it collects less often (696 against 1,353 collections) and expands instead. At 16 MiB the heap never needs to grow and peak RSS is unchanged.

The effect did not appear on a real form page: `GET /posts/new` (full render with these tags, through the generated `:web` pipeline) with this PR, #1456 and #1457 together peaked at 15.03 MiB at an 8 MiB heap against 16.33 MiB before, with 305,624 -> 22,072 bytes and 88.6 -> 64.8 µs CPU per request.

Merging is a call on whether a 3 MiB collector-sizing effect on a bare full-render route outweighs about 30% less CPU per render.

## Specs
- The five tags render once per manifest and return the same `String` afterward; 200 further rounds allocate under 64 bytes per round (rendering them afresh costs several kilobytes).
- A reloaded manifest starts empty; a missing asset raises every time and stores nothing; tags with attributes and public URLs are not stored; an edited import map hash renders afresh.
- `RenderedTags`: one render per key, kinds kept apart, the 1,024-entry limit.

title: Add Amber::Pipe::Compression with pooled zlib streams
body:
Crystal's `HTTP::CompressHandler` creates a new zlib stream for every compressed response, and `Compress::Deflate::Writer` gives zlib `GC.malloc` as its allocator. Each response therefore took about 270 KB of zlib state and buffers from the collected heap, which made the generated `CompressedResponsePipe` the largest allocation in an Amber CLI app: POST /posts, answered with a 302 through `:web`, allocated 309,857 bytes per request.

`Amber::Pipe::Compression` writes the same bytes, but its zlib streams come from `malloc`, outside the collected heap, and go back to a small pool when the response closes (`idle_compressors:`, 4 by default; a stream beyond that is freed at once, and one dropped without closing is freed by its finalizer). It decides on the first write exactly as the stdlib handler does (gzip first, then deflate, nothing when the response already has a `Content-Encoding`), answers range requests uncompressed and adds `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, like the generated pipe. `Content-Encoding: deflate` follows the compiler it is built with: a zlib stream from Crystal 1.22.0 on (as `HTTP::CompressHandler` and RFC 9110 do), bare DEFLATE data before.

Request bodies are untouched: #1454's refusal runs in `Pipeline#call` before any pipe, and a spec checks that a compressed request body is still answered 415 in a pipeline that plugs this pipe.

An Amber CLI app can keep its `CompressedResponsePipe` name and make it `class CompressedResponsePipe < Amber::Pipe::Compression; end`; amber_cli will generate that once it pins an Amber commit with this pipe.

## Measurements
Harness: `home-page-memory-bench` (`mem.rb`, `mem_post.rb`) on an app from Amber CLI main with the Post scaffold and 50 seeded rows; `crystal-alpha build --release` (Crystal 1.21.0, LLVM 21.1.8), arm64 macOS, production mode, one process, oha with `accept-encoding: gzip, compress, deflate, br`, 32 connections, 20 s. Before = amber v2-dev 814705ee with the generated `CompressedResponsePipe` around `HTTP::CompressHandler`; after = the same app whose `CompressedResponsePipe` subclasses this pipe. Three rounds per side, interleaved ABBA; medians. The machine was shared with heavy jobs (load average 40 to 270), so requests/s and p99 are approximate; bytes per request and CPU time per request are the steadier figures.

Generated default heap (`gc_initial_heap_mib: 16`):

| Route | Metric | Before | After |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| GET full page, gzipped | Bytes allocated per request | 299,887 | 23,050 (-92%) |
| | Server CPU per request | 62.1 µs | 55.7 µs |
| | Requests/s | 6,872 | 7,995 |
| | p50 | 2.05 ms | 1.86 ms |
| | Peak RSS | 23.08 MiB | 22.31 MiB |
| POST /posts (302, form + CSRF) | Bytes allocated per request | 309,965 | 33,112 (-89%) |
| | Server CPU per request | 84.7 µs | 74.7 µs |
| | Requests/s | 5,565 | 6,076 |
| | p50 | 2.81 ms | 2.44 ms |
| | Peak RSS | 26.28 MiB | 25.47 MiB |

Starting heap 0 (first batch, same method): GET full page 299,867 -> 23,050 bytes per request, p50 2.45 -> 2.11 ms, peak RSS 14.17 -> 13.16 MiB, 2,111 -> 941 collections in the first pair; POST /posts 309,935 -> 33,108 bytes, p50 3.21 -> 3.14 ms. p99 moved both ways between rounds under the shared load (POST 51.6 vs 56.4 ms in the medians above, 24.2 vs 32.1 ms in the first batch) and showed no direction.

## Specs
- Byte-for-byte equality with `HTTP::CompressHandler` for gzip and deflate on one small write, one long write, many writes, an empty write, 70 KB of random bytes, and a flush after the first write (the gzip modification time blanked on both sides). Passes on crystal-alpha 1.21 (bare DEFLATE) and Crystal 1.22 (zlib-framed).
- Round trips through the readers at levels 0, 1, 4 and 9; gzip preferred over deflate; no compression without `Accept-Encoding`, for a range request, after a flush that sent the headers, or when `Content-Encoding` is already set.
- The pool returns and reuses its stream, keeps at most `idle_compressors`, and the pipe allocates at least 200 KB less per response than `HTTP::CompressHandler`.
- A compressed request body is still refused with 415 through a pipeline that plugs the pipe.
